strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: scalable foundation modeling for volumetric CT using only openly available data. The combination of 3D transformer design, self-supervised pretraining, and report-level vision-language alignment is relevant and potentially useful to both medical imaging and representation learning communities.

The architecture is technically plausible and described with useful detail: anisotropic 3D patching, local-window ViT processing, global scan-level aggregation, 3D RoPE, DINO/iBOT/KoLeo pretraining, and SigLIP-style alignment are all reasonable adaptations to CT constraints.

The empirical scope is broad. The manuscript evaluates frozen biomarker classification, semantic segmentation, and text-to-image retrieval, which gives a more complete picture than a single downstream benchmark.

The retrieval results are compelling in parts: on CT-RATE, SPECTRE substantially improves over CT-CLIP, and on Merlin it improves over Merlin for Impressions retrieval and full-report settings, suggesting meaningful cross-modal alignment.

The supplementary material gives substantial implementation detail for datasets, preprocessing, training hyperparameters, model scale, and hardware, which helps reproducibility if the promised code/model release is made available.
weaknesses: A major concern is possible pretraining/evaluation contamination for segmentation. The pretraining corpus explicitly includes AMOS and other public abdominal datasets, while downstream segmentation is evaluated on AMOS-CT, LiTS, KiTS23, and WORD. The paper does not clearly state that downstream validation/test scans were excluded or deduplicated from SSL pretraining. Even unlabeled exposure to evaluation images can materially affect a foundation-model segmentation evaluation, especially when the claim is representation transfer.

The biomarker classification results are underreported in the main paper: Figure 1/Figure 3 show plots, but the manuscript does not provide exact AUC values per model/task in a table. This makes it difficult to verify the stated superiority on 4/6 tasks, assess effect sizes, or compare statistical overlap across models.

The ablation evidence is too narrow for the central technical claims. Table 7 only studies optimizer/crop size and SSL versus VLA on one KiTS23 fold for segmentation. There is no convincing isolation of key proposed components such as local-global hierarchy, 3D RoPE, anisotropic tokenization, DINO-style stochastic shifts, SigLIP versus CLIP/InfoNCE, text rewriting, model scale, or data scale.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled. Segmentation baselines are partly copied from different papers and protocols, and SPECTRE is integrated into nnU-Net with its own tuning choices. The paper frames gains as encoder-quality evidence, but differences in preprocessing, crop size, tuning, and training protocol may confound the comparison.

The segmentation results are competitive but not clearly state-of-the-art: SPECTRE trails nnU-Net/ResEnc on AMOS, KiTS23, and WORD, and only modestly improves on some transformer baselines. This weakens claims that the model broadly outperforms prior CT foundation/segmentation models.

The text-to-image retrieval comparison is mixed. SPECTRE is far below Merlin on Findings retrieval on Merlin, and the paper's discussion emphasizes settings where SPECTRE wins without sufficiently analyzing this failure mode.

Reproducibility remains uncertain despite detailed hyperparameters. The code availability line is blank in the extracted manuscript, and training requires 24 B200 GPUs plus GPU Direct Storage. Public release of weights would mitigate this, but the review must evaluate the submitted manuscript rather than promised future release.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, including 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models' and 'establishing SPECTRE' as a general foundation model. The evidence is promising, but gaps in contamination control, ablations, and exact reporting keep the contribution near the acceptance boundary rather than clearly above it.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: scalable foundation models for volumetric CT that combine self-supervised visual learning with report-level vision-language alignment. The focus on open datasets is valuable for a domain where many strong models depend on private clinical data.

The overall system design is plausible and technically coherent: local 3D ViT processing, scan-level aggregation, 3D RoPE, DINO/iBOT-style SSL, and SigLIP-style image-text alignment are reasonable choices for CT volumes and noisy radiology reports.

The manuscript evaluates on multiple downstream axes: frozen biomarker classification, semantic segmentation, and text-to-image retrieval. The CT-RATE retrieval gains over CT-CLIP are large, and the segmentation results are competitive with several transformer baselines.
The supplementary material gives useful implementation detail on datasets, preprocessing, model scale, training schedules, and hardware, which helps assess the practical setup.
weaknesses: The evidence does not adequately support the breadth of the claims. The method is mostly a careful combination of existing components, but the paper provides almost no ablation isolating the contributions of the proposed architecture, 3D RoPE/jittering, local-global split, DINO stage, SigLIP stage, report rewriting, or Qwen text encoder. The only substantive ablation is a KiTS23 optimizer/crop-size study, which does not establish why SPECTRE itself works.

There is a serious evaluation-contamination concern. The pretraining corpus includes AMOS CT scans, and the downstream segmentation evaluation also uses AMOS-CT. The manuscript does not state that downstream validation/test scans were excluded from pretraining. This undermines the segmentation evidence and any claim of clean transfer on that benchmark.

Several comparisons are not as fair or controlled as the writing suggests. Many segmentation baselines are imported from prior papers rather than rerun under the same preprocessing, training budget, and tuning protocol. The paper also tunes on KiTS23 fold 0 and excludes it, while baselines have different tuning histories. For retrieval, the Merlin table reports SPECTRE full-report results but does not show a directly comparable Merlin full-report result, and SPECTRE is worse than Merlin on Findings retrieval despite the discussion emphasizing cross-modal strength.

The headline segmentation claim is overstated. SPECTRE is below nnU-Net on AMOS and below nnU-Net ResEnc on KiTS, LiTS, and WORD where available. Its advantage is mainly over several transformer architectures, not over the strongest established 3D medical segmentation systems.

The biomarker evaluation is underreported. The main paper uses a radar plot and the supplement shows bars with confidence intervals, but exact numerical values, fold definitions, statistical tests, and sensitivity to kNN choices are not clearly presented. Several datasets are small, and the paper itself notes large confidence intervals on some tasks, so the claim of consistently superior representation quality is stronger than the evidence warrants.

Reproducibility is weak despite detailed training descriptions. The main page has a blank 'Code available at:' field, the nnU-Net/SPECTRE integration is promised only upon acceptance, and the training requires 24 B200 GPUs plus GPU Direct Storage. The LLM report-rewriting pipeline depends on Gemini and radiologist-curated examples that are not fully specified, making exact reproduction difficult.

The manuscript contains presentation and technical polish issues that reduce confidence: formatting artifacts, a blank code link, awkward or incorrect labels such as the local-attention cost being called global, and some imprecise statements such as claiming robustness from RoPE without direct evidence.

Overall, the paper has a worthwhile direction and some promising results, but the combination of limited causal evidence, possible downstream leakage, uneven baseline control, and overstated conclusions makes the current submission fall on the rejection side for CVPR.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and difficult problem: scalable foundation modeling for volumetric CT, where token count, anisotropy, and weak report supervision are real technical barriers.
SPECTRE is a strong practical system: a local/global 3D ViT, 3D RoPE, DINO-style SSL, and SigLIP-style report alignment are combined into a coherent CT-specific pretraining pipeline.

The pretraining scale is substantial for open CT data, with 229,619 CT series and paired-report training from CT-RATE, INSPECT, and Merlin. This is a meaningful community contribution if the promised model/code release is complete.

The evaluation is broad: frozen biomarker classification, semantic segmentation, and text-to-image retrieval. The reported results are consistently competitive, with strong gains over CT-CLIP on CT-RATE retrieval and good performance across several segmentation datasets.

The supplement provides many useful implementation details, including preprocessing, hyperparameters, architecture scale, hardware, downstream protocols, and some confidence intervals for biomarker results.
weaknesses: The main novelty is mostly in scaling and integration of known components rather than a clearly new learning objective or architecture. DINOv3, SigLIP, RoPE, local-window attention, and Qwen embeddings are sensible choices, but the paper needs stronger ablations to show which parts are essential.

Evaluation hygiene is a concern. The pretraining corpus includes AMOS and other public abdominal datasets, while downstream segmentation also evaluates on AMOS, LiTS, KiTS, and WORD-like public benchmarks. The paper does not clearly document de-duplication or exclusion of downstream validation/test cases from SSL pretraining, which weakens claims of generalization.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled. Segmentation baselines are largely taken from prior papers with differing protocols, model sizes, tuning, and pretraining resources, while SPECTRE benefits from very large-scale pretraining and substantial compute.

Ablations are limited. The only detailed ablation is on KiTS23 fold-0 for optimizer/crop/SSL-vs-VLA initialization. There is little direct evidence isolating the impact of the local/global hierarchy, 3D RoPE jitter, text rewriting, SigLIP vs CLIP, pretraining data scale, or freezing schedule.

Reproducibility is promising but not yet fully demonstrated in the manuscript. The code footnote appears incomplete, the nnU-Net integration is stated to be released upon acceptance, and training requires 24 B200 GPUs plus specialized I/O, making independent replication difficult even with open data.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. For example, “SOTA-level” and “outperforms prior CT foundation models” are partly task-dependent: SPECTRE is not best on all biomarker tasks, is below Merlin on Merlin Findings retrieval, and is competitive but not clearly superior to nnU-Net ResEnc on segmentation.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: scalable foundation modeling for volumetric CT using only openly available datasets, with both image-only and image-text pretraining.

The proposed SPECTRE system is technically plausible: a local/global 3D ViT design, anisotropic tokenization, 3D RoPE, DINO-style SSL, and SigLIP report alignment are sensible adaptations to CT memory and geometry constraints.
Evaluation is broad across frozen biomarker prediction, semantic segmentation, and text-to-image retrieval, rather than relying on a single downstream task.

Empirical results are promising in several places: strong CT-RATE retrieval gains over CT-CLIP, best or near-best frozen biomarker performance on several tasks, and competitive segmentation despite a lightweight encoder-centric decoder.
The supplementary material provides useful training details, dataset lists, hyperparameters, hardware, and decoder ablations, including an honest analysis showing small-lesion limitations.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited. Most ingredients are adaptations or combinations of existing components: ViT windowing/global aggregation, DINO/iBOT/KoLeo, SigLIP, Qwen embeddings, LoRA, and 3D RoPE. The paper would be stronger with clearer evidence that the specific combination, rather than scale alone, is responsible for the gains.

Ablation evidence is incomplete for the main claims. There is little isolation of local/global architecture choices, 3D RoPE jittering, text augmentation, SigLIP versus CLIP-style losses, SSL-only versus VLA across all downstream tasks, and the effect of pretraining scale/data composition.

Some headline claims are overstated relative to the tables. SPECTRE does not dominate retrieval on Merlin Findings, trails CT-FM on some TotalSegmentator settings, and is below nnU-Net ResEnc on the main segmentation table. The contribution is still useful, but the wording sometimes implies broader superiority than the evidence supports.

Data contamination and overlap risks are not fully resolved. The pretraining corpus includes aggregated public abdominal CT datasets, while downstream segmentation uses public benchmarks and TotalSegmentator-style data; aside from dropping AMOS, the manuscript does not clearly document patient/study-level de-duplication against all evaluation sets.

Segmentation gains are modest and mixed. SPECTRE improves over several transformer baselines but remains below strong convolutional nnU-Net ResEnc, and the small-structure analysis shows very poor detection of sub-10 mm masses for the lightweight decoder.

The biomarker evaluation is difficult to fully assess from the main paper because exact numerical AUCs are mostly shown graphically, and stronger statistical comparisons between SPECTRE and close baselines are not provided.

Reproducibility is weakened by blank or missing code/model URLs in the manuscript, reliance on very large 24-B200 pretraining hardware, and use of Gemini-generated report paraphrases without enough detail to reproduce or audit the generated text. Promised public release is valuable but cannot be assumed in the review.

Report rewriting and appending EHR code descriptions may improve alignment, but the manuscript gives limited analysis of whether this introduces label leakage, hallucinated clinical facts, or benchmark-specific shortcuts.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: scalable foundation models for volumetric CT, combining 3D self-supervised learning and vision-language alignment using only publicly available datasets. The focus on open CT data is valuable for the community if the release is actually provided.

The proposed system is practically ambitious: a large local/global 3D ViT design, DINO/iBOT/KoLeo-style SSL, SigLIP report alignment, Qwen-based text encoding, and evaluation across biomarkers, segmentation, and text-image retrieval.

Some empirical results are encouraging. SPECTRE substantially improves over CT-CLIP on CT-RATE text-to-image retrieval, performs best on several frozen biomarker tasks in the reported benchmark, and is competitive with transformer segmentation baselines despite a lightweight encoder-centric decoder.

The supplement gives useful implementation details on pretraining data, preprocessing, model scale, hyperparameters, hardware, and some ablations, including decoder variants and robustness analyses for retrieval.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited relative to the scale of the claims. Most components are adaptations or combinations of known recipes: ViT with 3D RoPE, DINOv3/iBOT/KoLeo-style SSL, SigLIP, LoRA-tuned Qwen embeddings, local-window plus global aggregation. The paper does not convincingly isolate which design choices are essential or novel for CT.

The main claims are overstated compared with the evidence. The paper repeatedly claims consistent outperformance and SOTA-level transfer, but segmentation does not surpass strong convolutional baselines such as nnU-Net ResEnc L, TotalSegmentator results trail CT-FM on two reported settings, and Merlin is substantially better on Findings-to-image retrieval. The evidence supports usefulness, not clear dominance.

The experimental comparisons are not uniformly fair or controlled. Several segmentation baselines are taken from prior work rather than rerun under the same pipeline, training budgets and tuning histories differ, KiTS fold 0 is used for development and excluded, and SPECTRE-specific hyperparameter choices are explored while baseline adaptation details are limited.

Ablation support is weak for a paper whose contribution is largely architectural/training design. There is no clean decomposition of local/global transformer design, 3D RoPE and jitter, DINO-only vs SigLIP alignment across all tasks, Qwen text encoder choice, report rewriting, window count, patch anisotropy, or pretraining data scale. As a result, it is hard to know what actually drives the gains.

Reproducibility is concerning despite the stated open-source intent. The code URL in the manuscript appears blank, LLM report rewriting depends on Gemini with radiologist-curated examples not fully specified, large-scale training requires 24 B200 GPUs and GPU Direct Storage, and many key evaluation details are deferred or described at a high level.

The biomarker evaluation is underreported in the main paper. The central claim is based largely on a radar plot and supplementary bar figure rather than exact tabulated numbers, statistical tests, or clear confidence interval values. Several tasks have small sample sizes and large uncertainty, making the claimed superiority fragile.

The vision-language evaluation is narrow. Retrieval is tested mainly on CT-RATE validation and Merlin test splits, both related to datasets used during training, and does not assess broader clinical language tasks, zero-shot classification, report generation, or external institution generalization. The full-report Merlin result lacks direct comparison to Merlin itself.

The segmentation design intentionally predicts at 1/4 resolution and the authors acknowledge smoothing and poor tiny-lesion sensitivity. The small-structure analysis shows extremely low Dice and low detection rates for lesions under 10 mm, which is clinically important and materially limits the usefulness of the proposed encoder-only segmentation setup.

Presentation sometimes masks limitations with broad language. Terms such as fully transformer-based foundation model, scalable path, global health equity, and consistent improvements are not always matched by rigorous evidence. The paper would benefit from a more restrained framing and clearer separation between demonstrated results and aspirations.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: scalable foundation models for volumetric CT. The proposed SPECTRE system is ambitious, combining a fully transformer-based 3D architecture, geometry-aware tokenization/RoPE, local-to-global attention, DINO-style SSL, and SigLIP-style report alignment.

The empirical scope is strong. The paper evaluates frozen biomarker classification across six public oncology benchmarks, dense segmentation across several CT datasets, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval on CT-RATE and Merlin. This breadth supports the claim that the representation is useful beyond a single downstream task.

Results are generally compelling. SPECTRE is best on 4/6 biomarker tasks, substantially improves CT-RATE retrieval over CT-CLIP, performs competitively for segmentation despite a deliberately simple encoder-centered decoder, and shows robustness analyses for report noise and voxel spacing.

The work emphasizes open/public CT data rather than private institutional-scale data, which increases community value. The supplementary material gives useful detail on pretraining datasets, preprocessing, hyperparameters, architecture scale, hardware, and downstream protocols.

The discussion is mostly appropriately calibrated: the authors acknowledge thoracic pretraining skew, report noise, compute cost, and the weakness of the encoder-only segmentation path for small lesions.
weaknesses: The novelty is partly incremental. Many ingredients are adopted from recent vision and medical foundation-model practice, including DINO/iBOT/KoLeo, SigLIP, Qwen embeddings with LoRA, 3D RoPE, and hierarchical local/global aggregation. The main contribution is convincing system scaling and integration, but the paper provides limited evidence that each architectural choice is essential.

Ablation evidence is incomplete for the central claims. There is no clear main-paper decomposition of SSL-only vs VLA, local/global design, 3D RoPE/jittering, text rewriting, data scale, or report/code inputs on the major downstream tasks. Without these, it is hard to tell whether gains come from architecture, data scale, objective choice, text model, or preprocessing.

Some evaluation claims are stronger than the tables support. SPECTRE does not uniformly outperform prior models: it trails Merlin on Merlin Findings retrieval, trails CT-FM on TotalSegmentator variants in the supplement, and remains below strong convolutional nnU-Net ResEnc for segmentation. The contribution is still useful, but the language around outperforming prior CT foundation models should be more carefully bounded.

Potential data overlap and contamination are not fully resolved. The authors note dropping AMOS for segmentation because it was used in pretraining, but other aggregated public datasets such as AbdomenAtlas and AbdomenCT-1K may overlap with downstream segmentation sources or related public benchmarks. The manuscript should more explicitly audit overlap at patient/study level for KiTS, LiTS, WORD, and TotalSegmentator-style evaluations.

Reproducibility is promising but not yet fully demonstrated. The paper says code is available, but the visible link appears blank in the manuscript, and another supplementary code reference also appears as a placeholder. Pretraining also uses very large hardware and Gemini-based report rewriting, which may be difficult to reproduce exactly without released processed text, prompts, and generated paraphrases.

The medical report augmentation pipeline could introduce subtle factual errors or distribution shifts. The paper states radiologist-curated examples and fact-preserving prompts, but does not quantify paraphrase fidelity or evaluate the effect of LLM rewriting against no rewriting on retrieval and downstream performance.

Some downstream protocols are not ideal for isolating broad representation quality. Biomarker evaluation relies on kNN over frozen embeddings and the exact numeric results are mostly shown graphically rather than tabulated in the main paper. Segmentation evaluation is complicated by decoder choices and training budgets, and the small-lesion analysis shows very weak detection rates for lightweight decoders.
